title: What times two thirds makes one?
description: One divided by two thirds is turned into a multiplication with a missing number. The missing number must bring a top and a bottom that match what two thirds already has. Keeko raises the doubt of dividing the one by the two.
teaching_notes: One idea: to make a product of one, the missing fraction needs the numbers that match every top and bottom of the fraction we divide by. Watch for students who divide the tops and forget the bottoms.

video_script.why: A learner sees how a division by a fraction becomes a multiplication with a missing fraction that makes the product one.
video_script.substitution: the numbers of the book's own second division, one and two thirds
video_script.anchor: one divided by two thirds written beside two thirds times a missing fraction equals one
video_script.wrong_move: divides the one by the two and ignores the three
video_script.payoff_line: One divided by two thirds is three halves
video_script.fraction_reading: two thirds, three halves, one half, one third
maths_rules: the missing top is 3 and the missing bottom is 2
video_script.design: A division and a multiplication with a missing fraction, joined by a double arrow. The two thirds is shown with room for a top and a bottom of the missing fraction.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; the division 1 ÷ 2/3 on the board

marks.pose: the division arrives on the board
marks.ask: a question mark glows beside the division

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about dividing by a fraction.
<bookmark mark='pose'/>Find one divided by two thirds, by asking what number times two thirds gives one.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is one divided by two thirds?

beats.on_screen: the division stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: 1 ÷ 2/3 = ? beside 2/3 × ? = 1, joined by a double arrow

marks.link: the division and the multiplication are joined by a double arrow

narration: <bookmark mark='link'/>Every division can be turned into a multiplication with a missing number.
<bookmark mark='one'/>To get a product of one, every number on top must match a number below.

marks.given: the two numbers are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers are one and two thirds.

marks.find: the words To find and the division are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find one divided by two thirds.

marks.write: the division is rewritten as a multiplication with a missing fraction

narration: <bookmark mark='write'/>Step one, write the division as a multiplication with a missing number, two thirds times what is one?

beats.on_screen: 2/3 × (missing top)/(missing bottom): the missing top must hold a 3; the missing bottom must hold a 2

marks.top: an arrow joins the three below to a space on top of the missing fraction
marks.bottom: an arrow joins the two above to a space below the missing fraction

beats.colours: the matching numbers in the accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step two, the missing top needs a three, to shorten the three below.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>The missing bottom needs a two, to shorten the two above.

marks.check: the product is written with tops over bottoms
marks.one: a tick shows the product is one

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step three, check by multiplying, two times three on top and three times two below.
<bookmark mark='one'/>Six over six is one, so this missing number works.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>One divided by two thirds is three halves.
That is one and a half.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 1 ÷ 2 = 1/2; then the check 1/2 × 2/3 = 2/6 = 1/3 is written beside it and crossed

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows the one divided by the two
marks.slip: the check is written and the result one third is crossed
marks.fix: the three is added to the top of the missing fraction

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we divide the one by the two, so the answer is one half.
<bookmark mark='slip'/>But one half times two thirds is one third, not one.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The missing number must also bring in the three, so it is three halves.
